before: An open book and a quiet place give this reader time to consider his question. This imagined contemporary scene invites patient study before deciding what a passage means. Joseph and Oliver’s account also begins with a question awakened while reading.
after: An open book and a quiet place give this reader time to consider his question. Joseph and Oliver’s account also begins with a question awakened while reading. What question would you like to take into your own study?

before: The detailed narratives were recorded after the event. Reading their dates and source notes helps us distinguish the remembered experience from the later work of writing Church history. The artwork accompanying this study offers an interpretation of that testimony, not an authenticated view of John's face or the exact clearing where they prayed.
after: The detailed narratives were recorded after the event. Reading their dates and source notes helps us distinguish the remembered experience from the later work of writing Church history.

before: Two young men bring groceries to a woman at her doorway. This imagined moment of care invites us to consider Alma’s call to bear one another’s burdens and ask what would help someone near us.
after: Two young men bring groceries to a woman at her doorway. Consider Alma’s call to bear one another’s burdens. What would help someone near you today?

before: At Haran, Jehovah promises Abraham that all families of the earth can receive gospel blessings through his seed. This illustration portrays the premortal Savior according to Latter-day Saint belief.
after: At Haran, Jehovah promises Abraham that all families of the earth can receive gospel blessings through his seed. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

before: data-full-image-alt: A devotional scene of Jesus Christ supporting a weary man’s arm on a wet rocky path.
after: data-full-image-alt: Jesus Christ supports a weary man’s arm on a wet rocky path.

before: alt: Devotional interpretation of Jesus Christ with disciples in a boat on choppy water
after: alt: Jesus Christ with disciples in a boat on choppy water

before: The Lord strengthens Alma’s people to bear their burdens before He leads them out of bondage. Two neighbors sharing a heavy basket give that strength an everyday form. Their task and surroundings are an artistic interpretation of the passage.
after: The Lord strengthens Alma’s people to bear their burdens before He leads them out of bondage. As you look at these neighbors sharing a heavy basket, consider how help can make a burden easier to bear.

before: The book of Moses records Adam’s baptism and spiritual rebirth. The landscape, clothing, and kneeling posture are artistic choices.
after: Adam kneels beside the water. Read how the book of Moses connects his baptism with the Spirit and new life.

before: A visit, a shared meal, an honest conversation, a moment of prayer: the imagined present-day scenes below bring discipleship into ordinary life. Let them help you consider one small way to follow Christ, with patience for the needs and pace of the people around you.
after: A visit, a shared meal, an honest conversation, a moment of prayer: discipleship takes shape in ordinary life. Consider one small way to follow Christ, with patience for the needs and pace of the people around you.

before: A quiet lane leads toward a farmhouse in this imagined early nineteenth-century setting. The scene recalls rural Harmony, Pennsylvania, where Oliver Cowdery sought assurance and received the Lord's tender command to look to Christ in every thought.
after: A quiet lane leads toward a farmhouse. Turn to the account from Harmony, Pennsylvania, where Oliver Cowdery sought assurance and received the Lord’s tender command to look to Christ in every thought.

before: Begin with those witnesses and the questions they actually answer. The opening artwork shows an imagined contemporary priesthood blessing. The historical account below traces a different moment: the restoration of authority through Peter, James, and John. The surviving sources do not establish a precise date for the conferral.
after: Begin with those witnesses and the questions they actually answer. The opening picture shows a priesthood blessing today. The historical account below traces a different moment: the restoration of authority through Peter, James, and John. The surviving sources do not establish a precise date for the conferral.

before: Books and notes rest together on a quiet desk in this imagined study scene. Take time with the witnesses: notice when each account was written, whose words it preserves, and what it helps you understand.
after: Books and notes rest together on a quiet desk. Take time with the witnesses: notice when each account was written, whose words it preserves, and what it helps you understand.

before: Two men sit together in a garden, one speaking while the other listens. This imagined moment invites us to consider how patience and gentleness can shape the way we serve someone.
after: Two men sit together in a garden, one speaking while the other listens. How might patience and gentleness shape the way we serve someone?

before: Which details do the scriptural and historical sources establish? Which details in the pictures are an artist’s interpretation? Keep both lists so a familiar picture does not become your evidence.
after: Which questions do the scriptural and historical sources answer? Which remain open? Keep those questions beside you as you compare the witnesses.

before: The Beloved Son stands with His hand over His heart, attentive to His Father. This devotional interpretation looks to His willing response before mortal life.

Moses records the Son’s acceptance of the Father’s will and His desire that the glory belong to the Father. Read the contrast in these verses carefully. Our study of settled faith begins with the Redeemer’s love and willingness, not with a claim that human resolve saves us. The unseen setting is an artistic interpretation of the premortal account.
after: The Beloved Son stands with His hand over His heart, attentive to His Father. Read His willing response before mortal life.

Moses records the Son’s acceptance of the Father’s will and His desire that the glory belong to the Father. Read the contrast in these verses carefully. Our study of settled faith begins with the Redeemer’s love and willingness, not with a claim that human resolve saves us.

before: The original artwork is a devotional interpretation. Scripture supplies the accounts; faces, clothing, settings, and the precise arrangement of people are artistic choices. Contemporary scenes illustrate daily discipleship.
after: Read the linked scriptures alongside each account, then consider how settled faith can shape daily discipleship.

before: The pictures give visible settings to these recorded encounters. Clothing, architecture, and the physical form of the record are artistic interpretations; the linked passages provide the account we study.
after: Open the linked passages and follow each encounter in its own setting. Notice what the witnesses tell us about the Savior and the hope His Resurrection brings.

before: A keepsake rests in her hands as she turns toward Him. This devotional scene invites us to bring sorrow to Christ and to listen with care when another person mourns.
after: A keepsake rests in her hands as she turns toward Him. Consider how you might bring sorrow to Christ and listen with care when another person mourns.

before: Each picture accompanies a passage you can open and read. The woodland landscapes, homes, clothing, and temple architecture are artistic interpretations inspired by Eastern Woodland settings, including Hopewell traditions; they do not establish where Book of Mormon events occurred. The scripture remains the source for what happens in each account.
after: Each picture accompanies a passage you can open and read. The scriptures do not settle the precise locations of these events in the ancient Americas. Follow the people and their choices in each account without treating a familiar landscape as evidence of where they lived.

before: A mother and son turn toward one another in an imagined quiet conversation. Later, the young warriors remember their mothers’ teaching with confidence. Read the words they carry with them, and consider how faith grows through ordinary conversations at home.
after: A mother and son turn toward one another in quiet conversation. Read how the young warriors remember their mothers’ teaching, and consider how faith grows through ordinary conversations at home.

before: The account helps us see the connection between a prophet preserving a witness for future readers and a young man entrusted with bringing that witness forth. The precise hand positions and arrangement of an illustrated meeting are an artist’s interpretation; the history centers on the record received and the responsibility attached to it. Continue with the Joseph Smith and Restoration study to follow that history, or return to the Book of Mormon’s invitation to come to Christ.
after: The account helps us see the connection between a prophet preserving a witness for future readers and a young man entrusted with bringing that witness forth. Follow the history of the record received and the responsibility attached to it. Continue with the Joseph Smith and Restoration study to follow that history, or return to the Book of Mormon’s invitation to come to Christ.

before: Two figures face the morning beside cultivated ground and a simple altar. This imagined scene of Adam and Eve invites us to read the promise of redemption they received.
after: Adam and Eve stand beside cultivated ground and a simple altar. Read the promise of redemption they received, and consider how hope in Christ shapes the work of an ordinary day.

before: Ancient faces, clothing, buildings, visions, and dreams are depicted through respectful artistic interpretation. Their exact appearance is not established by these texts. Look for what a passage records, what the picture helps you notice, and what remains a question.
after: Follow the scriptural promises and witnesses surrounding the birth of Jesus Christ. As you read, notice what each witness tells us and what questions remain.

before: Jesus Christ meets an older man with attentive warmth. Their joined hands and shared gaze invite a moment of reflection on being known and welcomed by the Savior. Let this imagined encounter lead into the scriptural account of His personal invitation to those gathered around Him.
after: Jesus Christ holds an older man’s hands and meets his gaze. As you read His invitation to the people gathered around Him, notice the care He gives to each person. What does His welcome help you understand about coming to Him?

before: Joseph attends to the hat while Oliver listens and writes. This interpretation of an 1829 dictation setting invites us to consider the concentration, trust, and practical work involved in receiving and recording the text. Historical accounts guide the scene; they do not preserve this exact session.
after: Joseph holds the hat close to his face while Oliver writes. Read the accounts of translation, and notice how the witnesses describe the work of dictating and recording the text. What did each person see and hear?

before: These details belong in a complete account, even when they differ from a familiar painting. An artist can help us imagine a room; the painting cannot decide which instrument was used at a particular moment. Likewise, a scribe could observe Joseph's posture, hear his words, and record them without seeing whatever Joseph reported seeing. Distinguishing outward observation from the claimed revelatory experience preserves the witnesses' perspective. It also avoids presenting a modern reconstruction as a photograph of something recorded in 1829.
after: These details belong in a complete account, even when they differ from a familiar painting. An artist can help us imagine a room; the painting cannot decide which instrument was used at a particular moment. Likewise, a scribe could observe Joseph's posture, hear his words, and record them without seeing whatever Joseph reported seeing. Distinguishing outward observation from the claimed revelatory experience preserves the witnesses' perspective. Each witness could describe only what was within that person’s experience.

before: Joseph and Emma share a warm glance as they walk along a quiet path. This imagined moment invites reflection on companionship beyond the work at a desk. Consider how making time to listen, speak kindly, and share an ordinary walk can strengthen a relationship.
after: Joseph and Emma share a warm glance as they walk along a quiet path. Consider how making time to listen, speak kindly, and share an ordinary walk can strengthen a relationship.

before: Open manuscripts lie side by side as a reader studies their pages in warm daylight. This imagined research setting invites patient comparison, attentive questions, and respect for the people who preserved the record. What can careful comparison teach us about the way a record reaches its readers?
after: Open manuscripts lie side by side as a reader studies their pages in warm daylight. What can careful comparison teach us about the way a record reaches its readers?

before: An ordinary offer of a ride becomes a remembered moment of sacred purpose in David’s later account. This artistic interpretation invites us to notice the person beside us. The faces, setting, and precise arrangement of the encounter are imagined, not a contemporary visual record.
after: David’s later account recalls an offer of a ride and an unexpected answer. Read his recollection, then consider how a brief encounter can stay with a person for years.

before: Mary’s later family account remembers encouragement in the midst of demanding household work. This interpretive scene honors that experience without claiming an authenticated likeness or an exact view of the plates. Whose quiet service could you notice, thank, or help carry today?
after: Mary watches as a visitor turns a leaf of the plates beside the barn. Her family’s later account remembers encouragement in the midst of demanding household work. Whose quiet service could you notice, thank, or help carry today?

before: Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris pause in an imagined conversation. Their different faces invite us to hear each witness as a person with his own history. Continue into their statements and the separate sequence of Martin’s reported experience, rather than treating this grouping as the angelic encounter.
after: Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris stand together. Read each witness’s statement, then follow the separate sequence of Martin’s reported experience. What does each man say he saw and heard?

before: A green coastal inlet opens between rugged hills and quiet water. This imagined landscape invites us to pause with the relief of reaching a place of abundance after a difficult journey. Consider the gratitude that can grow when a long road opens toward a new beginning.
after: A green coastal inlet opens between rugged hills and quiet water. Read about the travelers reaching a place of abundance after their difficult journey. What part does gratitude play when a long road opens toward a new beginning?

before: An aged record is held with care. Its pages preserve something of a person's life and faith. This imagined scene invites us to read those words patiently and learn how earlier disciples sought to follow Christ.
after: An aged record is held with care. Its pages preserve something of a person’s life and faith. Read those words patiently, and consider how earlier disciples sought to follow Christ.

before: A woman listens with an open notebook beside her scriptures. This imagined moment invites us to slow down with a conference message and consider one invitation to follow Jesus Christ.
after: A woman listens with an open notebook beside her scriptures. As you listen to a conference message, consider one invitation to follow Jesus Christ that you would like to remember.

before: The man meets Jesus after the restoration of his hand. This imagined moment of gratitude stays close to the personal care at the heart of Luke's Sabbath healing account.
after: The man faces Jesus with his restored hand. Read Luke’s account of the Sabbath healing, and notice how Jesus responds to the person before Him.

before: Amid the temple's upheaval, Jesus turns His attention to a person before Him. This imagined companion moment reflects on His compassion beside John's account of the cleansing; John does not record this particular conversation.
after: Jesus turns toward a person amid the temple’s upheaval. As you read John’s account of the cleansing, consider His concern for His Father’s house and the people who came there.

before: Jesus compares His presence with the joy of wedding companions while the bridegroom is with them. This imagined gathering illustrates that comparison, rather than the wedding at Cana or a portrait of Jesus.
after: Companions gather at a wedding. Read how Jesus compares His presence with the joy of wedding companions while the bridegroom is with them.

before: In this imagined scene, travelers pause beside a leafy fig tree and notice the green hillside. Jesus asks His hearers to observe the fig tree and other trees, recognizing summer's approach from their growth.
after: Travelers pause beside a leafy fig tree and notice the green hillside. Jesus asks His hearers to observe the fig tree and other trees, recognizing summer’s approach from their growth.

before: In the modern pictures, people plant, make bread, welcome others and choose how to spend their time. These imagined applications help us ask about patience, priorities and humble judgment. The kingdom parables remain our starting point; their promises belong to God's work, beyond what any one project may achieve.
after: People plant, make bread, welcome others, and choose how to spend their time. Bring those ordinary experiences to the kingdom parables as you consider patience, priorities, and humble judgment. Their promises belong to God’s work, beyond what any one project may achieve.

before: These imagined scenes bring neighborly care into everyday life. Consider what useful help might look like for the person before you: ask, listen and think about what continuing care may require.
after: Consider what useful help might look like for the person before you: ask, listen, and think about what continuing care may require.

before: Jesus asks which parent would give a child a stone when asked for bread. This imagined exchange pictures the ordinary care behind His comparison.
after: A parent offers bread to a child. Read Jesus’ question about a parent’s response to a child asking for food, and consider what it teaches about turning to the Father.

before: After Lazarus dies, Jesus describes him being carried by angels to Abraham's bosom, where he is comforted. This embrace pictures that comfort symbolically; its surroundings and bodily appearance are artistic choices, not a literal map of the afterlife.
after: After Lazarus dies, Jesus describes him being carried by angels to Abraham’s bosom, where he is comforted. Notice the embrace, then read how the parable contrasts his comfort with the rich man’s anguish.

before: Jesus speaks of salt retaining its savor and calls His listeners to have salt in themselves and peace with one another. This ordinary table setting offers a visual reflection on His words, not a recorded meal.
after: Salt rests on an ordinary table. Read Jesus’ words about retaining its savor, having salt in ourselves, and living at peace with one another.

before: Luke records a related saying in teaching about discerning the present time. The path toward the magistrate becomes a setting in which the need for timely action is visible. The picture does not dwell on the full legal dispute or tell us which modern procedure should be followed. Luke 12:58-59
after: Luke records a related saying in teaching about discerning the present time. The path toward the magistrate becomes a setting in which the need for timely action is visible. Consider why resolving a dispute promptly matters, while recognizing that this saying does not supply a modern legal procedure. Luke 12:58-59

before: A cup passes between two people while bread rests within reach. This illustration recalls the food and drink Jesus names among acts of care for another person's need.
after: A cup passes between two people while bread rests within reach. Read Jesus’ words about giving food and drink, and consider whose needs you might notice today.

before: A visitor sits close and holds the hand of a woman resting in bed. This imagined moment of companionship reflects Jesus' invitation to visit those who are sick.
after: A visitor sits close and holds the hand of a woman resting in bed. Read Jesus’ words about visiting the sick. What might it mean to offer someone your time and attention?

before: A visitor gives his attention to a man seated in confinement. This illustration recalls Jesus' words about visiting a prisoner and seeing a person others may overlook.
after: A visitor gives his attention to a man seated in confinement. Read Jesus’ words about visiting a prisoner, and consider how we see people others may overlook.

before: In Jesus' comparison, a person takes hold of the sheep and lifts it out. This imagined rescue pictures the ordinary care He uses to challenge resistance to doing good on the Sabbath.
after: A person takes hold of a sheep and lifts it out. Read Jesus’ comparison and His challenge to those who resisted doing good on the Sabbath.

before: The imagined present-day scenes bring stewardship into plans, shared resources and ordinary responsibilities. In the talents parable, the entrusted gift is money; applying it to our skills is a further reflection. Faithfulness asks how we use what we receive, without promising wealth, ease or status.
after: Stewardship reaches into plans, shared resources, and ordinary responsibilities. In the talents parable, the entrusted gift is money; applying it to our skills is a further reflection. Faithfulness asks how we use what we receive, without promising wealth, ease, or status.

before: The imagined modern scenes picture honest prayer, quiet preparation and attention to work that still needs doing. They invite us to remain faithful while we wait, even when a decision, recovery or other hoped-for outcome remains beyond our control.
after: Honest prayer, quiet preparation, and attention to unfinished work are ways to remain faithful while we wait. A decision, recovery, or other hoped-for outcome may still be beyond our control.

before: At the end of a shift or through a quiet hour, someone may still depend on a careful handoff or a promise kept. These imagined scenes ask us to notice the work entrusted to us now, even as we wait for something larger. Luke 12:35–38
after: At the end of a shift or through a quiet hour, someone may still depend on a careful handoff or a promise kept. Notice the work entrusted to you now, even as you wait for something larger. Luke 12:35–38

before: Jesus notices how guests choose places of honor and teaches them about humility. This imagined wedding gathering introduces the contrast between seeking prominence and taking a lower place.
after: Guests gather at a wedding. Read how Jesus notices their choice of places and teaches the contrast between seeking prominence and taking a lower place.

before: The risen Jesus eats before His disciples in Luke's account. This imagined indoor scene gives their astonished joy a personal focus, distinct from the shore breakfast in John 21.
after: The risen Jesus eats before His disciples. Read Luke’s account of their astonishment and joy, then compare it with the shore breakfast recorded in John 21.

before: The people minister to one another and hold things in common. Shared necessities give an imagined everyday form to the mutual care recorded after the Savior's ministry.
after: The people minister to one another and hold things in common. As you look at the shared necessities, consider how the Savior’s teaching changes the way people care for each other.

before: A hillside town remains visible above the valley. The imagined setting illustrates Jesus' comparison of His disciples to a city on a hill, within His teaching about good works that glorify the Father.
after: A hillside town remains visible above the valley. Read Jesus’ comparison of His disciples to a city on a hill. How can good works turn attention toward the Father?
